name: Ignatius of Loyola
role: Basque soldier turned priest, author of the Spiritual Exercises, founder and first superior general of the Society of Jesus (Jesuits)

born.place: Loyola castle, near Azpeitia, Gipuzkoa (Basque Country, Spain)

died.cause: Illness after years of poor health; an autopsy found gallstones, usually taken as the underlying cause

summary: Basque nobleman and soldier who, after a conversion during his recovery from a war wound, wrote the Spiritual Exercises and founded the Society of Jesus, which became a leading force in Catholic missions, education, and the Counter-Reformation.

key_dates.label: Leg shattered by a cannonball defending Pamplona against the French (20 May); conversion while convalescing at Loyola
Vigil at Montserrat; months of prayer and penance at Manresa (1522–23), where the Spiritual Exercises take shape
Pilgrimage to Jerusalem; the Franciscan custodian sends him back to Europe
Imprisoned by church authorities at Alcalá (42 days) and then at Salamanca (about 22 days) while his teaching was examined
Vows at Montmartre, Paris (15 August), with six companions including Francis Xavier and Peter Faber
Ordained priest in Venice (24 June); vision at La Storta on the way to Rome
Pope Paul III approves the Society of Jesus in the bull Regimini militantis Ecclesiae (27 September)
Elected first superior general of the Society (April)
Paul III approves the Spiritual Exercises; first printed edition
Founds the Roman College (later the Gregorian University)

accomplishments.text: Founded the Society of Jesus with companions from the University of Paris; approved in 1540, it grew to about 1,000 members by his death and became one of the largest Catholic religious orders.

Wrote the Spiritual Exercises, a month-long program of guided meditation and choice ('discernment') drawn from his own experience at Manresa, which became the basis of Jesuit formation and of retreats across the Catholic world.

Wrote most of the Society's Constitutions, which stressed mobility, obedience to superiors, and a special vow of obedience to the pope concerning missions, and dropped the choir office kept by older orders.
Turned the Society toward schooling: by his death it ran dozens of colleges, including the Roman College (1551) and the German College (1552), which trained priests for the Holy Roman Empire.
Sent Jesuits on missions abroad, beginning with Francis Xavier to India in 1541, and to Brazil, Ethiopia, and other lands.

Placed the Society at the service of the Counter-Reformation: Jesuits such as Diego Laínez and Alfonso Salmerón served as papal theologians at the Council of Trent, and Peter Canisius led Catholic renewal in Germany.

Recommended harsh measures against Protestants in the Habsburg lands in a 1554 letter to Peter Canisius, including removing heretics from office and teaching, burning their books, exile, and in some cases death.
Founded works of charity in Rome, including the House of Saint Martha (1543) for women leaving prostitution and a house for converts from Judaism.
Dictated an account of his life (the so-called Autobiography, 1553–55) to Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, the main source for his conversion and early years, written in the third person as 'the pilgrim'.

original.phrase: Ad majorem Dei gloriam (for the greater glory of God)
original.reference: Constitutions of the Society of Jesus, throughout
original.note: Phrases of this kind recur through his Constitutions and letters, and the Latin became the Jesuit motto (often abbreviated AMDG). Whether he coined the wording is not established.

original.phrase: Take, Lord, and receive all my liberty, my memory, my understanding, and my entire will.
original.reference: Spiritual Exercises §234 (the Suscipe, in the Contemplation to Attain Love)

original.phrase: Love ought to manifest itself more by deeds than by words.
What seems to me white, I will believe black if the hierarchical Church so defines.
original.reference: Spiritual Exercises §365, Rules for Thinking with the Church, rule 13

misattributed.phrase: Give me a child until he is seven and I will show you the man.
misattributed.note: Not found in his writings. Quotation dictionaries record it as an anonymous proverb attributed to the Jesuits in general, sometimes credited to Francis Xavier or Ignatius without a source.

misattributed.phrase: Pray as if everything depended on God; work as if everything depended on you.
misattributed.note: Not in Ignatius's own writings. It comes from a collection of maxims assembled by the Hungarian Jesuit Gabriel Hevenesi 150 years after his death, where the wording runs the other way ('Trust in God as if all success depended on you and not on God; yet work as though God alone will do everything'). The popular form is a later simplification.

persecution_note: Ignatius was repeatedly examined by church authorities while a layman preaching without theological training. He was imprisoned twice in Spain in 1527, at Alcalá and Salamanca, and investigated in Paris, Venice, and Rome; each case ended without a finding of heresy, but in Spain he was barred from teaching on matters of faith until he had studied. The Spanish Inquisition investigated him at Alcalá but did not try him. Later opposition, such as the Dominican Melchor Cano's attacks on the Exercises and the Paris Faculty of Theology's 1554 decree against the Society, was aimed at the order rather than at him personally.

persecution.title: Investigation and imprisonment at Alcalá
persecution.summary: At Alcalá, Ignatius and a few companions in grey habits gave spiritual instruction to townspeople, drawing suspicion that they were alumbrados (illuminists). Inquisitors from Toledo investigated and left the matter to the archbishop's vicar at Alcalá, Juan Rodríguez de Figueroa, who in 1527 had Ignatius jailed for 42 days while witnesses were heard, in part over two women who had gone on a pilgrimage, reportedly on his advice.

responsible.name: Spanish Inquisition (inquisitors of Toledo)
responsible.role: Investigated the group and referred the case to the vicar

responsible.name: Juan Rodríguez de Figueroa
responsible.role: Vicar general of the archbishop of Toledo at Alcalá; ordered the imprisonment

persecution.outcome: Released without a finding of error, but ordered to dress like other students and not to teach on matters of faith until he had studied further. He left for Salamanca.

persecution.title: Imprisonment at Salamanca
persecution.summary: Dominicans at the convent of San Esteban questioned Ignatius about how he could preach without study and held him there; he was then jailed, chained to a companion, for about 22 days by order of the bishop's vicar while judges examined his papers, including an early draft of the Exercises.

responsible.name: Dominican friars of San Esteban
responsible.role: Questioned him and reported him to the authorities

responsible.name: Vicar of the bishop of Salamanca (named Frías in the Autobiography)
responsible.role: Ordered the imprisonment and examined him with other judges

persecution.outcome: Judges found no error in his life or teaching but forbade him to define what is a mortal and what a venial sin until he had studied four more years. He left Spain for Paris.

persecution.title: Denunciations in Paris
persecution.summary: In Paris, students he influenced gave away their goods and changed their way of life, and Ignatius was denounced to the inquisitor; the principal of the Collège Sainte-Barbe, Diogo de Gouveia, threatened him with a public flogging, then relented. In 1535, hearing he had been accused again, Ignatius went to the inquisitor of France, Valentin Liévin, and asked for a judgment, which cleared him.

responsible.name: Diogo de Gouveia
responsible.role: Principal of the Collège Sainte-Barbe; threatened a public flogging

persecution.outcome: No punishment; a written declaration in his favor in 1535.

persecution.title: Heresy accusations in Rome
persecution.summary: After the companions criticized the preaching of the Augustinian Agostino Mainardi, Spaniards in Rome led by Miguel Landívar, a former follower, accused Ignatius and his companions of heresy and of having fled trials in Spain, Paris, and Venice. Ignatius refused a quiet dismissal of the charges and appealed to Pope Paul III for a formal verdict.

responsible.name: Miguel Landívar
responsible.role: Former associate who accused the group of heresy

responsible.name: Francisco Mudarra and other Spanish courtiers

defended_by.name: Pope Paul III
defended_by.role: Ordered the case to be decided after Ignatius appealed to him

persecution.outcome: The governor of Rome, Benedetto Conversini, pronounced them innocent in November 1538, after witnesses from their earlier investigations happened to be in Rome.

excommunication_note: Ignatius was never excommunicated or condemned. None of the investigations of 1526–1538 ended in a finding of heresy. He was beatified in 1609 and canonized by Pope Gregory XV in 1622. The Paris Faculty of Theology's decree of 1554 against the Jesuits condemned the Society, not Ignatius by name.
persecuted_others_note: Ignatius supported the use of church and state power against Protestants: he backed the refounding of the Roman Inquisition in 1542 and in 1554 recommended harsh measures against heretics in Germany, including in some cases death. He himself held no judicial office and is not known to have taken part in any trial or execution; he also resisted pressure to exclude men of Jewish descent from the Society of Jesus.

persecuted_others.title: Support for the Roman Inquisition
persecuted_others.targets: Protestants and suspected heretics in Italy
persecuted_others.summary: Pope Paul III re-established the Roman Inquisition in July 1542, a move led by Cardinal Gian Pietro Carafa (later Pope Paul IV). Ignatius supported the step and, by some accounts, urged the pope to take it; how much his advice counted is not clear.

persecuted_others.title: Letter to Peter Canisius on measures against heretics
persecuted_others.targets: Protestants in the lands of King Ferdinand of Austria
persecuted_others.summary: In August 1554 Ignatius wrote, at Canisius's request, advice for King Ferdinand: heretics should be removed from government and teaching posts, heretical books burned, and obstinate heretics punished, by exile or prison and in some cases death. He paired these with positive measures such as better preaching and the founding of colleges.
